core.one_sentence: Witherbloom is the school of life and death as a practical exchange system.
core.core_axiom: Life is not sacred because it is untouched; it is powerful because it can be spent, brewed, fed, healed, harvested, and returned.
core.player_fantasy: I understand the messy living system better than you do, and I will turn every gain, death, body, and bargain into pressure.
core.shadow: When unbalanced, Witherbloom becomes exploitative: everything alive is just fuel.

narrative_axes.question: Is death an ending or a conversion event?
Is the ecosystem being tended or harvested?
When does a creature stop being a person and become material?
Is this witchcraft folk knowledge, academic biology, or both?
What will Witherbloom protect, and what will it consume?

archetype_families.name: Body Ledger Aristocrats
archetype_families.summary: Creature death is not a failure state; it is the engine.

archetype_families.name: Cauldron Biology
archetype_families.summary: Food, potions, herbs, Pests, and bodily essence make the deck feel like field science and folk magic.

archetype_families.name: Growth from Life Change
archetype_families.summary: Life-total movement becomes counters, bodies, and combat pressure.

archetype_families.name: Compost Recursion
archetype_families.summary: The graveyard is not just death; it is soil, memory, and future material.
archetype_families.ui_language: the grave feeds the next organism

placement_copy_blocks.short: You read as Witherbloom: practical, loyal, earthy, and dangerous when life starts moving.
placement_copy_blocks.medium: Witherbloom treats life and death as one messy exchange system. You look for what is being fed, what is being spent, and what can grow from the cost.
placement_copy_blocks.deep: This placement is not just black-green recursion. It is biology as strategy: Pests, potions, life gain, sacrifice, rot, protection, and pressure. Witherbloom sees the battlefield as an ecosystem where every body has a future use.
